speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) whether regular assessments are conducted under the Hoarding Management Framework (HMF) to ensure that housing units of those assessed to be a threat to public health and safety under the framework do not pose as fire hazards to themselves and their neighbours; and (b) whether the current set of standard operating procedures under the HMF is adequate in ensuring that these housing units do not become a source of fire hazard.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) whether an update can be provided on the effectiveness of the implementation of the Hoarding Management Framework; and (b) whether it has reduced the number of reported hoarding cases in the last two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: First, I seek your permission to answer Question Nos 19 to 22 together?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Second, Members Mr Don Wee, Mr Murali Pillai1, Mr Melvin Yong2, Mr Desmond Choo3, Mr Gerald Giam4 and Ms Joan Pereira5 have also filed questions on the same topic which are scheduled for today and tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: My reply will effectively address their questions as well, and as such they may wish to withdraw their questions if their queries are answered today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: As such, may I request that the answers to both the MND and MHA PQs be provided first, and the supplementary PQs from Members on both sets of questions be taken together thereafter.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: While hoarders’ homes may be filled from floor to ceiling with what most may deem as "rubbish", they view these items as important and cannot bear to part with them.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In the most severe cases, the hoarder may even rough sleep outside their homes as there is hardly any space left inside.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Internationally, the Clutter Image Rating Scale (CIRS) is used to measure the extent and severity of hoarding.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The root cause of a hoarder's behaviour is complex.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, one's hoarding could be a symptom of underlying mental health conditions like Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD), or developed after trauma or deep grief.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hoarding behaviours could also be exacerbated by social factors, such as disputes with one's family or the stockpiling of collected items at home for one’s “karang guni” business.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: While hoarding is more often observed in the elderly, it is a behavioural trait that could have slowly deteriorated throughout adulthood and worsened as one ages.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hoarding can happen within the confines of one's flat, but can also spill out into common areas such as shared corridors.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: A hoarded home may be infested with pests from rotting food or pose a fire risk as occupants may be unable to escape in an emergency due to blockages to exit routes from the extreme accumulation of clutter.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hoarding that clutters corridors also obstructs evacuation routes for neighbours in times of fire.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The emanating stench may also inconvenience neighbours and be a nuisance by preventing them from enjoying living in their own homes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These public health and safety risks and dis-amenities warrant state intervention for the well-being of both the hoarder and the community.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Government has taken an inter-agency approach to address hoarding because of its complexity and potentially fatal public hazards.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The HMCG comprises HDB, NEA, the Animal and Veterinary Service (AVS) of NParks, SCDF, MSF, People's Association and the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC).

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In the Hoarding Management Framework (HMF), hoarding cases are assessed and prioritised based on whether there is threat to public health and safety.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where risks are identified to the extent that established rules and laws are violated, regulatory agencies will issue orders or take enforcement action on the hoarder or homeowner.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, NEA may order the owner to remove items contributing to pest infestations in their home, while SCDF may order the owner to cease hoarding flammable items, such as fuel.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: AVS will also act against hoarding of animals within a HDB flat where animal welfare is harmed, or Town Councils may require owners to remove hoarding in the common areas.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: HMCG considers community and social interventions in tandem with enforcement efforts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If the hoarder is suspected to have mental health issues, the hoarder will be referred to AIC and the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) for professional assessment and treatment.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Agencies work closely with healthcare workers, community partners such as social workers from Family Service Centres, grassroots leaders, volunteers and the hoarders' family members in a concerted effort to resolve hoarding cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, even with the involvement of mental health agencies and professionals, deep-seated issues may still result in recurrence as behavioural change is unlikely to happen overnight.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If your family member is a hoarder, we seek your strong support on agencies' efforts to declutter as family intervention has proven to be a major success factor in hoarding intervention.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These complex cases remain protracted and unresolved because it is difficult to gain hoarders' cooperation to declutter.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Frontline officers face real tensions on the ground in balancing between the person's individual right to choose how they want to upkeep their own home and their neighbours' enjoyment of their own residences, especially in cases where the clutter falls short of outright legal violations, or does not meet the threshold for public health and safety risks as determined by SCDF and NEA.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In such cases, officers need to obtain the cooperation of the hoarder to help them declutter.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This involves repeated engagements, persuasion and at times, referrals to social workers and/or mental health professionals.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We have encountered cases where hoarders refuse to open their door for inspections or cooperate in decluttering – some may even threaten self-harm at the thought of losing their belongings.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Even if their homes were successfully decluttered once, the clutter may recur as habits do not change so quickly.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, as recent cases have shown, decluttering is needed not just for the communities' safety, but to protect the individual's safety.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: HMCG will continue to work hard at this problem.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We empathise with neighbours' frustration with the recurrence of inconveniences and disamenities, but also seek your understanding that the challenges and complexities in hoarding intervention require persistent efforts sustained over a long period, both on agencies' and the hoarder's part.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In tandem, MSO will work with the media as well as social and grassroots workers to further spread and reinforce key messages through more Public Education on the dangers of hoarding and cluttered corridors.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will also continue to tackle known cases of egregious hoarding within flats.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will work with agencies to assess risks posed by the worst hoarding cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where orders are issued for public health and safety reasons and hoarders are cooperative, we will proceed to declutter via the community-based approach with the assistance of volunteer groups.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, even in cases where hoarders are unwilling to part with their items, we will act firmly in the interest of public health and safety to intervene.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We seek the understanding of the public that we cannot allow decluttering efforts to be blocked by the remonstrations of individuals who may be endangering public health and safety with their actions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Lastly, HMCG alone cannot identify all hoarding cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Residents who come across hoarding behaviour with public health and safety concerns may report such cases through the OneService App, which will then be referred to agencies for further assessment.
